section_title: The Gentle Servant and the Hope of the Nations

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 15 Aware of this, Jesus withdrew from that place. Large crowds followed Him, and He healed them all, 16 warning them not to make Him known. 17 This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah:

18 “Here is My Servant, whom I have chosen, My beloved, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will proclaim justice to the nations. 19 He will not quarrel or cry out; no one will hear His voice in the streets. 20 A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish, till He leads justice to victory. 21 In His name the nations will put their hope.”

context_lines: Aware of the plot against Him, Jesus withdraws. He continues healing the crowds who follow, while warning them not to make Him known. Withdrawal does not mean that His care for people stops. Matthew places His conduct within the words of Isaiah.

The passage draws from [Isaiah 42:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/42.htm): God's chosen Servant receives His Spirit, brings justice, and becomes the hope of the nations. Matthew explicitly identifies what Jesus is doing as fulfillment. The contrast with the preceding plot matters: His mission advances without taking on the character of His opponents.

The bruised reed and smoldering wick picture things already close to breaking or going out. The Servant does not finish their destruction. Gentleness is joined with determination: He will bring justice to victory. Care for the weak and the establishment of what is right belong to the same mission.

The reach of that mission is also clear. The nations will put their hope in Him. The quotation widens the reader's view beyond the immediate dispute, showing that the Father's purpose through Jesus extends far beyond the people gathered around Him on this occasion.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand Matthew as identifying Jesus with Isaiah's Spirit-given Servant, whose gentleness does not weaken His purpose to bring justice. [Wesley on Matthew 12:18–21](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) applies the fragile images to people burdened by sin and those with only a small beginning of hope. The [US Catholic bishops' notes on 12:15–21](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/matthew/12) emphasize Jesus' meekness and the mission reaching Gentiles. These are complementary emphases on the Servant's manner and the people His work reaches.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
god_plan_lines: The hope of the nations is part of God's promise before the conflict described here. In [Luke 2:25–32](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/2.htm), Simeon recognizes the infant Jesus as salvation prepared for all peoples, bringing light to Gentiles and glory to Israel. The wider mission grows from God's announced purpose.

That purpose becomes visible in the apostolic mission. Speaking to the Gentile household of Cornelius, Peter recalls Jesus being anointed with the Holy Spirit, doing good, and freeing people from oppression. He then announces His death, resurrection, and forgiveness for everyone who believes in Him ([Acts 10:34–43](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/10.htm)). The Servant's gentle ministry leads into good news carried across the nations.
